div.p:
C. K. Cumming
Titled Miss by Leonard Woolf in correspondence dating 1928-01-20. informs Leonard Woolf that she had declined Woolf's job offer as the Hogarth Press manager in hopes of a better position being offered from other firms, and now regrets the decision. She asks Woolf that, since he has connections in the publishing industry, if he could inform her of opportunities in any firms expanding their business, as her application would have a higher rate of success. Typescript letter signed by C. K. Cumming.

You may think it rather extraordinary that I should ask you for any help
See correspondences 1928-01-20 and 1928-01-24. The first letter was from Leonard Woolf, inviting C.K. Cumming to come work for him as Press Manager but in the second letter she declined., but things have come out very unhappily for me.
I think that the thing that really weighed most with me in January
See letters from 1928-01-20 and 1928-01-24. and caused all my vacil- lation and consequent wrong decision was the fact that I had previously had some dealing with another firm. I might want to accept it, and that I ought not to accept your post with that possibility in my mind. I can't think now why I ever thought I might prefer it and I have regretted a hundred times both my indecision and my over-scrupulousness.
Anyhow, after keeping me in suspense for weeks (it is months since the first conversation), they have finally decided to promote someone inside the firm instead (just what I might have expected) and the whole thing falls to the ground, a great disappointment.
This means that I have to begin again to canvass all the firms in London, which is very disheart- ening. It is so difficult to know the right moment.
What I thought I would ask you is this. As you are inside the publishing world, you might pos- sibly hear in advance that some firm was contemplating changes or expansion. An application under those cir- cumstances would stand a much better change of receiving attention. If you ever did hear of such a thing and would let me know, I should be immensly grateful, and would not use your name at all, if you did not wish it. I hope you will not think that I am taking too great a liberty in asking you.
